# Titus 1 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 1: "Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness"

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Servant (bondservant) of God":** The Greek word *doulos* is the most abject term for a slave — one who has surrendered his will entirely to his master. David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes it also carried the idea of a *slave by choice*, like the OT bondservant who had his ear pierced (Ex 21:1–6). Paul's first self-designation is not "apostle" but "slave of God." Donald Grey Barnhouse (cited at Precept Austin) connects this to the OT law: the freed slave who loved his master could voluntarily become a permanent bondservant, his pierced ear proclaiming his master's character wherever he went. (URLs: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/titus_11-9)

- Ellicott notes this opening is longer and more formal than Paul's greetings to Timothy, likely because his relationship with Titus was less intimate than with Timothy. (URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/1.htm)

- **"According to the faith of God's elect":** Ellicott insists the Greek preposition *kata* should be translated "for (the furtherance of) the faith" — the *purpose* of Paul's apostleship, not merely conformity to it. Precept Austin notes most modern translations follow this sense: "for the faith" (NASB), "to further the faith" (NET). (URLs: same as above)

- **"God's elect":** Ellicott offers four guiding principles: (1) arbitrary election to privilege exists in the visible world; (2) Scripture repeatedly teaches election in grace; (3) election does not cancel free agency — it is possible to refuse good and choose evil; (4) all references to the elect are meant as comfort for struggling believers, not stumbling-blocks. Precept Austin cites Hiebert: "although surrounded with mystery, the biblical teaching on election is for believers and is intended as a practical truth." (URLs: same)

- **"Knowledge (epignosis) of the truth that leads to godliness":** Precept Austin explains *epignosis* means full, precise, experiential knowledge — not mere head-knowledge but personal involvement with the truth. The truth Paul preaches is designed to produce godliness (*eusebeia*), a holy and useful life. (URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/titus_11-9)

**Reformed View (Ligonier):**
- Ligonier stresses that Titus is about "the truth that leads to godliness" — truth and godliness must always go together. The stress on truth and godliness continues throughout the letter. Paul's primary task was to preach the gospel so that the elect might reveal themselves by trusting in it and be built up in knowledge of God, which produces holy living. (URL: https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/3-things-titus)

**Baptist View (Desiring God / John Piper):**
- In "Look at the Book" labs on Titus 1:1–4, John Piper traces how Paul's aim is faith leading to truth and godliness. The incarnation, hope, and godliness form the overview of the letter. (URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/incarnation-hope-godliness-an-overview-of-titus)

---

## v. 2: "in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"In hope of eternal life":** Ellicott renders this "resting on the hope of eternal life." Paul's apostleship had for its object the faith of the elect and knowledge of the truth, and the *basis* on which all this rested was the hope of eternal life. (URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/1.htm)

- Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that eternal life is not merely a future state — it is the life of the Eternal God living within us now, to be completed later. Hope here is not wishful thinking but anticipation founded on a promise from the God who cannot lie. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"God, who cannot lie":** Ellicott suggests this striking phrase may have been chosen with reference to the peculiar Cretan vice — as v. 12 says, "Cretans are always liars." In contrast to the lying character of the people, God is utterly truthful. (URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/1.htm)

- **"Promised before time began":** Ellicott renders "from eternal ages." The promise of eternal life was the result of a divine purpose fixed from eternity (see also 2 Tim 1:9). (URL: same)

---

## v. 3: "In His own time He has made His word evident in the proclamation entrusted to me by the command of God our Savior."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"In His own time" (due time):** Ellicott translates "in His own seasons" — the fitting seasons fixed by God. Guzik notes Christianity entered the world at a uniquely opportune moment: a common language (Greek), Roman roads and peace (*pax Romana*), safe sea travel, and a world conscious of its need for a saviour. (URLs: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/1.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"Manifested His word through preaching":** Guzik stresses that preaching is God's chosen method to make His eternal word evident in the present. Paul does not shrink from calling his preaching the vehicle for God's word. (URLs: same)

- **"Entrusted to me by the command of God our Savior":** Ellicott notes the commandment came to Paul directly from God — on the Damascus road, in the temple at Jerusalem, in visions. Paul emphasises that he did not undertake this work from his own will. "God our Saviour" here refers to God the Father (as in 1 Tim 1:1), while the title is also ascribed to the Son in v. 4 — an indication of Paul's belief in the equality of the Son with the Father. (URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/1.htm)

---

## v. 4: "To Titus, my true child in our common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Titus himself:** Ellicott provides an extensive biography: Titus was a Greek, uncircumcised, probably converted by Paul at Antioch. He accompanied Paul and Barnabas to the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15; Gal 2:1–3) and was the living example of Gentile freedom from the Mosaic law. He later became Paul's trusted troubleshooter — sent to Corinth to handle that fractious church and complete the collection for the Jerusalem poor. (URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/1.htm)

- Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) said of Titus: "He seems to have been a man of great common sense; so that, when Paul had anything difficult to be done, he sent Titus." Guzik adds that Titus was a "true son," a genuine brother, a partner and fellow worker with Paul. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"My true child in our common faith":** Guzik notes that Paul stood for a *common* faith, not an isolated one. White (cited by Guzik) says the faith is "common to all Christians," like Jude 3. (URL: same)

- **"Grace and peace":** Note the BSB text omits "mercy" (present in KJV). Ellicott notes many older authorities omit "mercy" here. The source of all grace and peace is "God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior." Calvin (cited by Guzik) says: "The Son has brought to us salvation from the Father, and the Father has bestowed it through the Son." (URLs: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/1.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

---

## v. 5: "The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **Crete:** Ellicott notes Crete (modern Candia) was a large, populous Mediterranean island, mentioned in Homer as having 90–100 cities. It had many wealthy Jews and probably first received the gospel from Cretans present at Pentecost (Acts 2:11). The churches were numerous but disorganised. (URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/titus/1.htm)

- **"Set in order what was unfinished":** Wiersbe (cited by Guzik) notes "set in order" is a medical term — it was applied to setting a crooked limb. Things were crooked among the Cretan congregations and needed to be set straight. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"Appoint elders in every town":** Guzik notes Paul uses "elders" (*presbuteros*) in v. 5 and "overseer/bishop" (*episkopos*) in v. 7 interchangeably — both describe the same office. Calvin (cited by Guzik) wrestles with the authority Paul gave Titus: "He may seem to give Titus too much authority when he tells him to appoint ministers for all the churches. This would be almost royal power." Calvin suggests Titus merely ratified congregational choices, but Guzik counters that "there is not a hint of this in the text." (URL: same)

- Ligonier (Reformed): "Churches cannot safely remain without the ministry of pastors, and consequently, wherever there is a considerable body of people, a pastor should be appointed over it" (Calvin, cited in the Ligonier devotional). Being a centre for sea trade, Crete's churches particularly needed solid organisation to prevent doctrinal and ethical contamination, since travellers passing through would form lasting impressions of Christianity. (URL: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/elders-church-crete)

---

## v. 6: "An elder must be blameless, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Blameless":** Guzik explains the Greek literally means "nothing to take hold upon" — there must be nothing in the leader's life that others can seize to attack the church. Augustine (cited by Ligonier) clarifies: "Paul does not say 'If anyone is without sin.' For if he were to say this, every person would be rejected, no one would be ordained." Being above reproach is not sinless perfection but honesty about sin with evidence of repentance. (URLs: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/ ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/elders-church-crete)

- **"Husband of but one wife":** Guzik says the idea is "a one-woman man." It does not mandate marriage (otherwise Jesus and Paul would be disqualified), nor does it absolutely prohibit remarriage after a wife's death or biblical divorce. The point is that the leader's focus is on one woman — his wife. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"Having children who are believers":** Hiebert (cited by Guzik): "If they remained pagans, it would throw into question the father's ability to lead others to the faith." White (also cited by Guzik) notes the moral requirements for the pastor's children are more mildly expressed in 1 Timothy 3:4–5 — here in Titus the emphasis is on the children's submission to discipline and restraint. The Greek word for "dissipation" (*asotia*) is the same used of the Prodigal Son's riotous living (Luke 15:13) — wasteful, extravagant self-destruction. (URL: same)

---

## vv. 7–8: "As God's steward, an overseer must be above reproach — not self-absorbed, not quick-tempered, not given to drunkenness, not violent, not greedy for money. Instead, he must be hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"As God's steward":** The overseer manages God's household. The greater the Master, the greater the servants are expected to be. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **The negative list:** Guzik notes:
  - *Not self-willed*: Not "determined to have his own way in everything" (Clarke).
  - *Not quick-tempered*: The Greek *orgilos* refers more to a settled state of simmering anger — a bitter man — than an occasional flash of temper.
  - *Not given to wine*: Not one who drinks more than is proper.
  - *Not violent*: Barclay (cited by Guzik) notes the Greeks widened this word to include violence in speech — one who browbeats others.
  - *Not greedy for money*: White (cited by Guzik) notes no regulations for deacons are given in Titus, so "presbyters performed the duties of every church office. Hence they should have the appropriate deaconal virtue." (URL: same)

- **The positive list:** Guzik groups them: *just* (right toward men), *holy* (right toward God), *self-controlled* (right toward himself). Matthew Henry: "How unfit are those to govern a church who cannot govern themselves!" (URL: same)

- *Sober-minded* (also rendered "prudent" or "self-controlled"): Guzik says this describes one who thinks clearly, knows the value of things, and does not cheapen the ministry by foolish behaviour. Paul used this word ten times in the letters to Timothy and Titus. (URL: same)

---

## v. 9: "He must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Hold firmly to the faithful word":** Guzik gives three points: (1) the leader must be personally convinced of God's word and bring it with confidence, not mixed with academic doubts; (2) he must stick to the word rather than fads and programs; (3) "as he has been taught" means he has been discipled by someone else — not necessarily through seminary, but through being taught. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"Encourage... and refute":** Luther (cited by Guzik): "A preacher must be both soldier and shepherd. He must nourish, defend, and teach; he must have teeth in his mouth and be able to bite and fight." (URL: same)

**Reformed View (Ligonier):**
- The elder's firm grasp on true doctrine is essential because "all the teaching gifts in the world will not help the church if its appointed teachers do not guide the bride of Christ in understanding the health-giving truths of the Word of God." Calvin: "In a pastor there is demanded not only learning, but such zeal for pure doctrine as never to depart from it." The church should support theological education, provide means for ongoing pastoral training, and help pastors acquire resources. (URL: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/foundation-for-instruction)

---

## vv. 10–11: "For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision, who must be silenced. For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Many are rebellious (insubordinate)":** Guzik explains the Greek is the negative form of the word "submit" — these people will not submit to God's order of authority. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"Those of the circumcision":** Paul was particularly concerned with Christians from a Jewish background who taught that keeping the Law of Moses was the key to acceptance before God — a Jewish legalism. (URL: same)

- **"Who must be silenced":** Guzik says plainly: Titus had to train the elders to "shut up" these problem people. They should not be allowed a hearing, because if allowed they would "subvert whole households." (URL: same)

**Reformed View (Ligonier):**
- The presence of "teachers" who rebel against God's Word is precisely why the Lord ordained elders. Calvin: elders must "be on the watch, so as not to give silent permission to wicked and dangerous doctrines to make gradual progress." (URL: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/silencing-false-teachers)

- Ligonier also notes the connection to Paul's instruction in Titus 3:9–10 to "avoid foolish controversies" — there comes a time when divisive people must be dealt with decisively. Thomas Aquinas' commentary on Titus 3 is cited as an example: if someone maintains "God is not triune and one" or "fornication is not a sin," he is a heretic. (URL: https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/3-things-titus)

## vv. 12–14: "As one of their own prophets has said, 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.' This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith and will pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **The Cretan prophet:** Guzik identifies the quote as from Epimenides, a 6th-century BC Cretan poet and religious teacher. The Cretan reputation for lying was so notorious that the Greeks coined a verb *krētizein* — "to cretize" — meaning to lie and cheat. Paul endorses this pagan prophet's assessment: "This testimony is true." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"Rebuke them sternly":** Because of the hardened character of the Cretans, they needed direct, sharp rebuke. The goal was redemptive: "so that they will be sound in the faith." (URL: same)

- **"Jewish myths" and "commands of men":** The particular error troubling the Cretan churches was a Jewish legalism — not centred on God's word but on "Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn from the truth." (URL: same)

---

## vv. 15–16: "To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed."

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"To the pure, all things are pure":** Guzik explains that the false teachers, with their attraction to Jewish legalism, seemed to believe that *nothing* is pure. They denied Christians basic, godly pleasures that were not sinful — likely referring to ceremonial food laws and similar restrictions. Paul counters: purity or defilement is a matter of the heart, not external things. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

- **"Their minds and their consciences are defiled":** The problem is internal. The false teachers' understanding and moral sense have both been corrupted. (URL: same)

- **"They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him":** Guzik notes these people talked like Christians — their profession was in order — but their lives contradicted their words. Paul says we cannot go by what a person says alone; we must also look at how they live. (URL: same)

- **"Detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed":** These are strong words. Guzik suggests the false teachers probably pretended to a higher spirituality than Titus and the godly leaders. Paul saw through the façade and wanted the Cretan Christians to see through it too. (URL: same)

**Reformed View (Ligonier):**
- These false teachers "profess to know God, but they deny him by their works" — showing they are wrong in both lip and life, in teaching and behaviour. This is the opposite of what Paul requires of elders. (URL: https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/3-things-titus)

## Denominational Distinctives and Other Views

*Note: I was limited by the site's search/fetch caps and could not retrieve full pages from many denominational and "other views" sources. What follows is what the search excerpts yielded.*

**Reformed (Ligonier):** The Ligonier devotionals emphasise divine sovereignty in election (v. 1), the necessity of church order through elder governance (v. 5), and the absolute authority of sound doctrine to both encourage and rebuke (v. 9). The elder's role as "steward of God" is stressed, with blamelessness understood as ongoing repentance, not sinless perfection. (URLs: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/elders-church-crete ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/foundation-for-instruction ; https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/3-things-titus)

**Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper):** Piper's "Look at the Book" labs walk verse-by-verse through Titus 1, tracing how Paul's apostleship aims at faith leading to truth leading to godliness. The emphasis falls on the organic connection between doctrine and life. The Baptist contribution here does not appear to differ sharply from the traditional Protestant reading on the key points of Titus 1. (URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/incarnation-hope-godliness-an-overview-of-titus)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik's commentary (widely used in charismatic and evangelical circles) emphasises the practical, transformational power of the gospel to change even notoriously corrupt cultures like Crete. The focus is on godly character over mere gifting for leadership. The "bondservant" concept is highlighted as voluntary, joyful slavery to a great Master. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/titus-1/)

**Older Commentaries (Ellicott, Gill, Pulpit):**
- *Ellicott* (1870s, Anglican) gives careful attention to Greek prepositions, historical context (Crete's geography, Jewish population), and Titus's biography. He is particularly helpful on the translation of *kata* as "for the furtherance of" in v. 1, and on the phrase "God who cannot lie" as a deliberate contrast to Cretan character.
- *Gill* (Baptist, 18th century) — the search excerpt summarises: Titus was an uncircumcised Gentile, a man of great grace, dear to Paul, and the chapter concerns elder qualifications and the refutation of false teachers. (URL: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/titus/1.htm)
- *Pulpit Commentary* (1880s) — notes that "servant" is better than "slave" (contra Farrar), and that the letter is a public and official document conveying apostolic authority. On "the faith of God's elect," it suggests the phrase points to rising heresies, mainly from Jews, of whom there was a considerable colony in Crete. (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/titus/1-1.htm)

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions (from retrieved sources)

1. **The connection between truth and godliness** is the letter's central thread: sound doctrine inevitably produces godly living (v. 1).
2. **Leadership is about character, not gifting**: the elder qualifications (vv. 6–9) set a standard of spiritual maturity for all believers to measure themselves against.
3. **False teaching must be confronted directly**: Titus is told to silence deceivers (v. 11) and rebuke sharply (v. 13), but always with the redemptive goal of soundness in the faith.
4. **The Cretan cultural context** — notorious for lying, laziness, and vice — makes the gospel's transformative power all the more remarkable. Paul does not counsel Titus to seek easier ground but to transform these people through Christ.
5. **"God who cannot lie"** (v. 2) and "Cretans are always liars" (v. 12) form a deliberate contrast: the God of truth versus a culture of deception, and the gospel bridges the gap.
